title: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
tagline: Ionic and covalent bonds; Lewis structures; bond parameters; VSEPR shapes; valence bond theory and hybridisation; resonance; molecular orbital theory of diatomic molecules; hydrogen bonding.

Syllabus unit and chapter title were taken from the official-verified ISC Chemistry registry entry; no board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Atoms do not usually stay alone; they combine to form molecules and compounds. The forces that hold them together are chemical bonds. In this chapter we study the main kinds of bonding and the models chemists use to explain them. We start with ionic and covalent bonding and Lewis structures, move to bond parameters such as length, energy and polarity, then use VSEPR theory to predict molecular shapes. We also look at valence bond theory, hybridisation, resonance and the simpler parts of molecular orbital theory, and finish with hydrogen bonding and its effects.

facts.label: Core ideas
facts.value: Ionic and covalent bonding; Lewis structures; octet rule and its limits; bond length, energy, angle, order; polarity; VSEPR; valence bond theory; hybridisation; resonance; molecular orbital theory for simple diatomics; hydrogen bonding

learningOutcomes: Draw simple Lewis structures and use the octet idea carefully.
Explain bond parameters such as length, energy, angle and order.
Predict molecular shapes using VSEPR theory.
Describe hybridisation and use it to explain shape and bonding in simple molecules.
Explain the basic ideas of molecular orbital theory for first-period diatomic molecules.
Describe hydrogen bonding and its consequences.

blocks.text: An ionic bond is formed when one or more electrons are transferred from one atom to another, so that oppositely charged ions attract each other. A covalent bond is formed when atoms share electrons. Many bonds lie between these two extremes. The simplest descriptions come from thinking about valence electrons and whether an atom tends to lose, gain or share them in order to reach a more stable arrangement.

items: Ionic bonding involves electron transfer and electrostatic attraction.
Covalent bonding involves sharing of electrons.
Many bonds have both ionic and covalent character.
Electronegativity differences help judge the nature of a bond.

items.text: Sodium chloride forms when sodium loses an electron and chlorine gains one; the resulting Na+ and Cl- are held together by attraction. In Cl2, the two chlorine atoms share a pair of electrons, which is a covalent bond.
items.note: The same substances are not all purely ionic or purely covalent; bonding is best understood on a spectrum.

learn.title: Lewis structures and the octet idea

blocks.text: Lewis structures are electron-dot diagrams that show how valence electrons are arranged in a molecule. They are useful for keeping track of shared and unshared electrons. The octet rule says that many atoms are most stable when they are surrounded by eight valence electrons, but it is a guideline, not a universal law. Some molecules have fewer than eight electrons on an atom, and others have more. The structure is a model, and the model should be used with care.

items: Lewis structures show shared and lone pairs of valence electrons.
The octet rule is useful but not universal.
Some stable molecules have incomplete or expanded octets.
Formal charge can help choose the better Lewis structure.

items.text: In the Lewis structure of water, oxygen is surrounded by two bonding pairs and two lone pairs, making eight electrons around oxygen. In some molecules, such as those of boron or elements in higher periods, the octet rule does not apply in the simple way.
items.note: Lewis structures are bookkeeping tools; they do not by themselves explain shape or energy in full.

blocks.text: A covalent bond can be described by several parameters. Bond length is the average distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms. Bond energy is a measure of the strength of the bond. Bond angle tells how atoms are arranged around a central atom. Bond order gives an idea of the number of bonding electron pairs between two atoms. These parameters help explain why molecules have the shapes and stabilities they do.

items: Bond length is the average internuclear distance.
Bond energy measures bond strength.
Bond angle depends on the arrangement of electron pairs.
Bond order is related to the number of bonding interactions.

items.text: A double bond is generally shorter and stronger than a single bond between the same two atoms, because there is greater electron sharing between the nuclei.
items.note: Bond order and bond length go in opposite directions in the simple cases: higher order usually means shorter bond.

blocks.text: VSEPR theory predicts molecular shape by counting the electron pairs around a central atom and assuming they repel each other. The shape depends on both bonding pairs and lone pairs. Lone pairs generally repel more than bonding pairs, so they can change the bond angles away from the ideal values. The best way to use VSEPR is to count electron domains first, then decide the electron-pair geometry, and finally the molecular shape after ignoring the lone pairs.

items: VSEPR uses repulsion between electron pairs to predict shape.
Count bonding pairs and lone pairs around the central atom.
Lone pairs often reduce bond angles more than bonding pairs.
Electron-pair geometry and molecular shape are often different.

items.text: Ammonia has four electron domains around nitrogen, so its electron-pair geometry is tetrahedral, but one of these is a lone pair, so the molecular shape is trigonal pyramidal. Methane has four bonding pairs and no lone pairs, so its molecular shape is tetrahedral.
items.note: The key step is separating electron-pair geometry from molecular shape; confusing the two is a common mistake.

blocks.text: Hybridisation is a model that mixes atomic orbitals to form new hybrid orbitals suitable for bonding. It is one way to explain the geometry of molecules and the number of bonds formed by an atom. Different hybridisation schemes match different shapes: sp, sp2 and sp3 are common examples. Hybridisation is related to, but not the same as, VSEPR electron-domain count.

items: Hybridisation mixes atomic orbitals to make bonding orbitals.
sp, sp2 and sp3 are common types.
Hybridisation is used to explain geometry and bonding.
It is a model, not a physical process that can be directly observed.

items.text: In methane, the carbon is often described as sp3 hybridised, with four equivalent orbitals pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron. In ethene, carbon is often described as sp2 hybridised, with one double bond present.
items.note: Do not confuse hybridisation with electron-domain count; the two ideas are related but are used differently.

blocks.text: Some molecules cannot be described well by a single Lewis structure. In these cases, chemists use resonance, which means the real structure is a blend of several contributing structures. Molecular orbital theory takes a different approach: it builds molecular orbitals from atomic orbitals and fills them with electrons. For simple diatomic molecules, this model can explain bond order and magnetic behaviour more directly than a single Lewis structure.

items: Resonance describes a molecule as a blend of structures.
Resonance structures are not real, separate forms.
Molecular orbitals are built from atomic orbitals.
Bond order and magnetism can be read from a molecular orbital diagram.

items.text: A simple diatomic molecule can be described by filling bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals with electrons. If there are more electrons in bonding orbitals than in antibonding ones, a stable bond is predicted.
items.note: Molecular orbital theory is especially helpful when a single Lewis structure gives a poor picture of the molecule.

blocks.text: Hydrogen bonding is a special kind of attraction that occurs when a hydrogen atom is bonded to a strongly electronegative atom such as fluorine, oxygen or nitrogen and is attracted to another electronegative atom nearby. It is weaker than a covalent bond but much stronger than many other intermolecular attractions, and it has visible effects on properties such as boiling point and the structure of water and biological molecules.

items: Hydrogen bonding occurs with F, O or N bonded to hydrogen.
It is an intermolecular attraction, not a covalent bond.
It affects boiling points and the structure of molecules like water.
It is also important in biological systems.

items.text: Water has a higher boiling point than might be expected from its size because of hydrogen bonding between molecules. This same idea is one reason water has an unusual and important set of properties.
items.note: Hydrogen bonding is strongest when the hydrogen is attached to a very electronegative atom and is close to another electronegative atom.

keyPoints: Ionic bonding involves transfer of electrons and electrostatic attraction; covalent bonding involves sharing.
Lewis structures show shared and lone pairs; the octet rule is a guide, not a universal rule.
Bond length, energy, angle and order describe covalent bonds.
VSEPR predicts shape from electron pairs, including lone pairs.
Hybridisation is a model that explains geometry and bonding, especially sp, sp2 and sp3.
Resonance and molecular orbital theory help when one Lewis structure is not enough.
Hydrogen bonding is a strong intermolecular attraction involving H bonded to F, O or N.
examFocus: When predicting shape, count lone pairs as well as bonding pairs; the electron-pair geometry and the molecular shape are not always the same.
Do not treat the octet rule as absolute; some stable molecules have fewer or more than eight electrons around an atom.

vocabulary.meaning: A bond formed by electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, usually after electron transfer.
A bond formed by sharing electrons between atoms.
An electron-dot diagram showing shared and lone pairs of valence electrons.
A measure of the number of bonding electron pairs between two atoms, related to bond strength and length.
A model in which atomic orbitals mix to form new orbitals for bonding.
An intermolecular attraction involving a hydrogen atom bonded to a strongly electronegative atom such as F, O or N.

questions.prompt: A covalent bond is formed by:
questions.explanation: Covalent bonding involves sharing electrons between atoms.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing covalent bonding with ionic bonding, which involves transfer.

questions.prompt: Bond length is best described as:
options: The average distance between two bonded nuclei
The energy needed to break the bond
The number of bonds between two atoms
questions.answer: The average distance between two bonded nuclei
questions.explanation: Bond length is the average internuclear distance in a bond.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing bond length with bond energy or bond order.

questions.prompt: Why is ammonia trigonal pyramidal rather than tetrahedral?
questions.answer: Because ammonia has four electron domains around nitrogen but one of them is a lone pair, so the molecular shape formed by the atoms is trigonal pyramidal, not tetrahedral.
questions.explanation: The electron-pair geometry is tetrahedral, but the lone pair makes the atom positions form a trigonal pyramid.
questions.commonMistake: Ignoring the lone pair and calling the molecular shape tetrahedral.

questions.prompt: What is meant by resonance in a molecule?
questions.answer: Resonance means the actual structure is a blend of several Lewis structures, none of which alone describes the molecule accurately.
questions.explanation: Resonance structures are not real separate forms; they are contributing descriptions.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking the molecule flips between the resonance structures.

questions.prompt: Compare the molecular shapes of NH3 and CH4 and explain why they are different even though both have four electron domains around the central atom.
questions.answer: Both have four electron domains, so both have tetrahedral electron-pair geometry. In CH4 all four are bonding pairs, so the molecular shape is tetrahedral. In NH3 one domain is a lone pair, so the molecular shape formed by the atoms is trigonal pyramidal. Lone pair repulsion is greater and reduces the bond angle.
questions.explanation: The difference comes from the lone pair in ammonia; electron domain count alone does not determine the molecular shape.
questions.commonMistake: Equating electron-pair geometry with molecular shape and calling both tetrahedral.
